newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia car sales seen slipping after strong run.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia car sales seen slipping after strong run.

text.p: After chalking up 44.4 percent growth in 1995, car sales in Malaysia rose 22.5 percent last year and the increase is expected to shrink further in 1997, a motor trade group said on Thursday.

Slower economic growth, high interest rates and tighter monetary policy were expected to curb sales this year to growth of eight percent, the Malaysian Motor Traders Association (MMTA) said in its annual report.

"We are always conservative in our forecast, but this is because the industry is dependent on several factors and cannot continue growing at this rate forever," MMTA chairman Aishah Ahmad told reporters after presenting the report.
A total of 275,615 cars were sold in 1996, compared with 224,991 in 1995.
The MMTA a year ago had forecast sales growth of 8.5 percent for 1996, far under the 22.5 percent recorded in the annual report.
The trade group forecast that passenger car sales would rise by eight percent to 297,664 in 1997.
Aishah said the MMTA was more optimistic about the commercial vehicle sector, which saw sales rising by 47 percent last year owing to a boom in infrastructure services.

"Our members are of the view that with the prevailing buoyant economy, and the many mega-projects in the pipeline, (sales of) commercial vehicles are expected to improve in 1997," Aishah said. The MMTA forecast commercial vehicle sales to grow 23 percent this year.
Motor stock analysts concurred with the association's views, but were more bullish on their projections.
"I think we'll see an 18 percent growth in passenger car sales and 30 percent in commercial vehicles this year," said Mazuin Ahmad, an auto analyst at Caspian Research.
"Imported luxury cars and four-wheel-drives are also expected to do well as incomes rise," she said.

Motor industry executives said demand for heavily taxed imported cars such as the Mercedes Benz, BMW, Volvo and Honda, and luxury four-wheel-drives such as Range Rover and the Chrysler Jeep, had grown in Malaysia, although total market share for these was below 10 percent.
Locally made cars, led by the Proton, still monopolised sales in 1996, with a market share of 80.9 percent, the MMTA said.

"I think we're definitely looking at a slower year for passenger cars in 1997, with a growth of between 10 and 15 percent, which is still healthy given that it's a faster growth rate than the economy," said Rene Low, an auto analyst at research house Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
Malaysia is in its ninth straight year of more than eight percent growth, which is expected to be sustained at around eight percent at least until the year 2000.
The government has forecast economic expansion of 8.2 percent in 1996 and eight percent in 1997, down from the 9.5 percent growth recorded in 1995.
